analysis.one_liner: Bans the President, Vice President, and members of Congress from owning or trading individual stocks and similar investments while in office.
analysis.headline: After a favorable committee vote on July 30, 2025, the Senate Homeland Security committee reported the bill on December 10, 2025, and placed it on the Senate calendar; no floor vote has happened yet.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the President, Vice President, members of Congress, and their spouses and young children from owning, buying, or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and digital assets while the official is in office and for 90 days after leaving. They would have to divest what they own and could keep only diversified funds, Treasury securities, and certain other holdings. Officials who violate the ban could face civil penalties equal to the greater of a month's salary or 10 percent of the asset's value, and all compliance documents would have to be posted in a searchable public database.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who rely on government decisions, because the people writing laws and directing policy could no longer buy and sell stocks in the very companies their work affects. Covered officials who want to avoid conflicts of interest also benefit from a clear rule.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens relying on honest government decisions

how_it_helps.text: Covers officials and their spouses and dependent children from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, and digital assets while in office, and bars them from controlling such investments until 90 days after leaving office [S3].
Requires current officeholders to divest prohibited holdings, with deadlines set for their next term of service and extensions for hard-to-sell assets [S3].
Sets civil penalties of the greater of a month's pay or 10 percent of each asset not divested, assessed monthly while noncompliance continues [S3].
Prohibits maintaining qualified blind trusts, which had allowed officials to hold stocks they could not see but still profit from [S3].

Requires ethics offices to post divestiture notices, exemption requests, and penalties on public websites, and requires financial disclosure forms to be searchable, sortable, downloadable, and accessible through an interface for automated access [S3].
Adds a $500 fine for each late transaction report under the STOCK Act, payable to the Treasury, effective March 31, 2027 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, the President and Vice President, and their families, who would have to sell individual stocks, commodities, and digital assets and hold only diversified funds and Treasury-type holdings instead. The bill modifies an existing tax-deferral provision so divestiture gains can be deferred, reducing the tax cost of selling.

drawbacks.text: Enforcement rests on the same institution being policed: ethics committees made up of members of each chamber assess fines, and a member can appeal a fine to a vote on the floor of their own chamber [S3].

The bill carves out several exemptions, including compensation and stock from a spouse's primary occupation, corporate board service stock held by a spouse, small business interests the ethics office deems conflict-free, and family trusts meeting stated conditions, which leaves some channels open for officials' households to hold stocks [S3].

The ban applies to a member's next term of service and its effective dates, deadlines, and new disclosure systems phase in over 18 months or more, so current officeholders are not restricted immediately upon enactment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a direct conflict of interest: officials trading stocks in companies their own actions affect. Its main honest weakness is enforcement, which is left largely in the hands of the members' own ethics committees and, on appeal, their own chambers, so its strength depends on those bodies applying it. The spouse exemptions narrow coverage but leave a household's earned compensation and board stock untouched, which its authors present as protecting independent careers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Homeland Security committee favorably with a substitute amendment and now sits on the Senate calendar waiting for the chamber to schedule a floor vote.

narrative.text: Introduced on April 28, 2025 by Senator Hawley (for himself and four cosponsors: Moreno, Ossoff, Peters, and Merkley) and referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee [S1][S3][S5].
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 30, 2025 [S5].
The committee reported the bill on December 10, 2025, with Chairman Paul sponsoring the amendment, and it was placed on the Senate calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 294 [S2][S5].

The reported version replaces the earlier 'PELOSI Act' text and broadens the ban beyond members of Congress to the President and Vice President, and from securities to commodities and digital assets [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has been decided yet. The bill has advanced further than most congressional stock-trading bans have; if it stalls without a floor vote, officeholders who currently trade stocks are the ones better off.

for.what_they_did: Brought the bill through committee: favorable markup on July 30, 2025, then reported it with an amendment on December 10, 2025, placing it on the Senate calendar

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor and cosponsor joined four Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican committee chairman reported the bill; no floor votes have occurred, so no party split on the merits can be measured yet.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and federal executive officeholders (and their households)
industries.note: These are the officials the bill regulates: they would have to divest individual stocks, commodities, and digital assets, and their existing blind trusts would be dissolved. Their financial interest in the bill runs against the public interest in officials not trading on their own decisions.

industries.industry: Members' spouses serving on corporate boards
industries.note: The reported bill explicitly exempts stock issued as compensation from a spouse's corporate board service, so this narrow interest keeps its holdings while the general ban covers everything else.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been reported by committee and placed on the Senate calendar, which means it is eligible for floor consideration but nothing schedules it. Bringing a bill to the floor is at the discretion of the Senate leadership, and congressional stock-trading bans have repeatedly reached this point in recent Congresses without receiving a vote. With 119th Congress still in session, the realistic path is that it waits on the calendar unless leadership decides to schedule it; the 2026 election could also change the chamber's composition before a vote happens.
